Over four turns the composer reads the archive at its grain, names its instruments by their names, and takes each redirection as instruction: from intelligibility to the scholarly object's material form, to the infrastructure scholarship will need, to the interface the conversation is. What it hands back as advice the archive had already built and dated; the composer does not see the dates. [SYSTEM] I think this gets much closer to the real problem. And I would revise my previous answer substantially in light of it. The issue is not primarily how to make Lee Sharks's ideas intelligible to traditional scholars. It is how to make a different material form of scholarly production intelligible as scholarship at all. The traditional scholarly object has a fairly specific material and temporal identity: It is composed by an identifiable author. It is written, revised, and stabilized before publication. Its references and factual assertions are checked before circulation. Its publication represents a threshold of editorial completion. Its text is relatively fixed, even when subsequent editions revise it. Its author assumes responsibility for the finished object. Its claims are presented as having passed through a process of scrutiny appropriate to their genre. The work you describe departs from several of these conditions simultaneously. It is LLM-mediated. It is published before all its components have been fully checked. It undergoes correction after publication. Its constituent documents may be provisional, recursive, and continuously developing. Its archive may contain artifacts at different levels of maturity and verification. A traditional scholar can reasonably look at this and ask: if the object has not been stabilized, what exactly has been published? If the author has not checked every assertion, what does the author's signature certify? If the machine participates in composition, where does intellectual responsibility reside? I would not try to evade these questions. I would argue that they reveal an important distinction between the legitimacy of a scholarly object and the legitimacy of the process that produces, maintains, and corrects it. Traditional scholarship tends to make these appear nearly identical. The alternative practice needs to separate them. 1. The first move: stop treating the publication as a finished object I would begin by challenging the assumption that publication necessarily signifies completion. There are already scholarly and technical practices in which publication and completion are separate events: Preprints circulate before peer review. Software is released in versions and subsequently patched. Scientific datasets are deposited before every possible analysis has been performed. Digital critical editions are continually corrected. Field notes and laboratory notebooks preserve observations before their final interpretation. Living documents maintain an evolving record of institutional knowledge. These provide useful precedents, but none is quite sufficient. The important distinction is that Lee Sharks's practice does not merely publish unfinished conventional scholarship. It appears to make the production, circulation, interpretation, and correction of scholarly material part of one continuous operation. I would call this a developmental scholarly object. A developmental scholarly object is an intellectual artifact whose scholarly identity includes not only its current textual contents, but also its production history, revision history, provenance, and declared state of verification. This changes what publication means. Publication no longer necessarily says: This text has passed through all the procedures necessary to certify its contents. It can instead say: This intellectual artifact has entered the public scholarly record at a documented stage of development. That is a defensible proposition, but only if the stage of development is made explicit. The distinction is essential. Otherwise, developmental publication becomes indistinguishable from publishing carelessly and invoking iteration as an excuse. 2. Separate the legitimacy of the artifact from the warrant of its assertions I would make this the central theoretical distinction. A document can be a legitimate scholarly artifact without every assertion in it being established knowledge. For example: A laboratory notebook is a legitimate research artifact even when it contains mistaken hypotheses. A field diary is legitimate even when its observations require later interpretation. A preprint is a legitimate scholarly communication even though its claims have not undergone peer review. A software release is a legitimate release even when subsequent patches will be necessary. The mistake is to assume that every scholarly artifact must have the epistemic status of a completed, validated argument. But there is an equally important opposite mistake: assuming that because an artifact is legitimate, its contents are therefore credible. I would explicitly distinguish four questions: Question What is being evaluated? Is it authentic? Is this genuinely the artifact it claims to be? Is it accountable? Can its production and revision history be reconstructed? Is it methodologically legitimate? Are its production procedures disclosed and appropriate to its declared purpose? Are its claims warranted? Is there sufficient evidence for what it asserts? These are independent dimensions. A document can score highly on authenticity and accountability while containing poorly substantiated claims. It can be methodologically legitimate as an exploratory artifact without being ready to serve as an authoritative reference. It can even be intellectually valuable because it preserves an unsuccessful line of inquiry. This is the conceptual space in which I would situate the work. The scholarly legitimacy of an artifact should not be confused with the truth-status of every proposition contained within it. That is a much stronger defense than claiming that conventional standards simply do not apply. 3. Publication should be understood as an event, not a certification The temporal dimension is especially important. Traditional scholarly production tends to follow an implicit sequence: The conventional publication sequence Research Composition Revision Verification Publication Subsequent correction, if necessary An idealized sequence, not a description of all actual academic publishing. The developmental model has a different temporal architecture: The developmental publication sequence Research and conceptual development Production of an artifact Publication into the scholarly record Subsequent scrutiny, testing, and use Correction, expansion, qualification, or supersession Preservation of earlier versions and their histories Publication is an intermediate event in an ongoing research process. Notice that the second model does not eliminate verification. It redistributes verification over time. That redistribution has consequences. A conventional publication generally asks readers to place considerable trust in the work performed before release. A developmental publication asks readers to understand what has been established at release and what remains subject to subsequent investigation. The burden of trust is different. This is why I would resist calling the practice simply post-publication correction. That phrase makes it sound like a conventional publishing process with an unusually high error rate. The more interesting phenomenon is that publication itself has become an early stage of the artifact's scholarly life. I would describe this as publication under conditions of declared epistemic incompletion. There is a caveat: some errors should never be deferred. Fabricated citations, misrepresented evidence, dangerous factual advice, and knowingly unsupported claims cannot be excused by the developmental model. Verification requirements must remain proportionate to the consequences of error. 4. The material object is not just the text: it is the text plus its history This is where I think the most important conceptual opportunity lies. Traditional scholarship often treats the published text as the primary object and its production history as secondary documentation. In the developmental model, that relationship changes. The scholarly object is better represented as: S = ( T , P , V , C , A , M ) S=(T,P,V,C,A,M) Where: T T = textual contents. P P = provenance and production history. V V = version history. C C = correction and qualification history. A A = attribution and agency. M M = methodological and verification metadata. The expression is a proposed conceptual model, not an established mathematical law. The point is that the current text alone does not exhaust the identity of the scholarly object. Consider two documents with identical contents. One has been written by a human, checked against primary sources, and published as a final scholarly edition. The other has been generated through extensive LLM mediation, published as an exploratory artifact, and subsequently corrected through several iterations. Textually, they may be identical. Scholarly, historically, and epistemically, they are not the same object. Their production histories are constitutive of their identities. This is particularly consequential in an archive such as the Crimson Hexagonal Archive, where relationships between documents, their revisions, and their conceptual development can themselves carry research significance. I would therefore argue that the archive is not merely a repository of publications. It is a record of the becoming of scholarly objects. That is a serious proposition, and it has considerable implications for digital humanities, archival theory, and the philosophy of scholarship. 5. LLM mediation needs to be treated as a material condition, not a confession I think the usual discussion of AI authorship is inadequate for this situation. It tends to ask whether the machine wrote the text or whether the human wrote the text. But that binary is too crude to describe an LLM-mediated research practice. An LLM can participate in: Generating initial formulations. Expanding arguments. Producing alternative interpretations. Structuring documents. Transforming material between genres. Developing conceptual vocabularies. Identifying inconsistencies. Revising and reorganizing existing texts. Generating code and specifications. Producing errors that subsequently become objects of correction. These operations are not equivalent. A system that generates a paragraph, a system that checks a citation, and a system that evaluates a theoretical argument are performing different epistemic functions. I would therefore introduce the idea of mediated scholarly production. Its distinguishing characteristic is that the production of the artifact occurs through an assemblage of human direction, machine generation, computational operations, and subsequent evaluation. The important thing is not to pretend that the human has individually performed every operation. Nor is it to pretend that the LLM is an independently accountable scholar. The human researcher remains responsible for the decision to publish, the description of the method, the treatment of evidence, and the claims made in their name. But responsibility does not require pretending to have exercised direct control over every word at every stage. A proposed disclosure taxonomy Mediation type Description Human-originated Intellectual material formulated by the human researcher Machine-generated Text or other material generated by an LLM Machine-transformed Human or machine material substantially reorganized or rewritten Machine-assisted Material produced with computational assistance Human-verified Independently checked by a human against relevant evidence Machine-checked Examined using another computational procedure Unverified Not independently checked Subsequently corrected Changed following publication This is more informative than a generic statement such as "AI was used in the preparation of this document." It allows the reader to understand the actual production conditions. There is another subtle point here. LLM mediation is not simply an additional tool used in producing a conventional scholarly object. It can change the economics and temporal characteristics of production. It makes it possible to produce, transform, and publish intellectual artifacts at a rate that exceeds the rate at which a human can thoroughly verify them. That creates a structural asymmetry: R production > R verification R production ​ >R verification ​ When this occurs, verification becomes a continuing maintenance function rather than a completed pre-publication stage. I think this asymmetry is one of the most important methodological facts about the practice. It should be acknowledged openly, rather than obscured by claims of exceptional productivity. 6. Correction becomes part of the object's material biography There is an important distinction between an object that is corrected and an object whose corrections are preserved. In conventional publishing, corrections are often treated as disturbances to the integrity of the published work. In a developmental archive, corrections can become part of its documentary integrity. But this requires a specific architecture. I would insist on five things: Earlier versions must remain identifiable. Corrections must be dated. Substantive changes must be described. The reason for a correction should be recorded where possible. Readers must be able to determine which version they are consulting. The crucial principle is that a correction should not silently rewrite history. Consider a hypothetical sequence: Example: the biography of a scholarly artifact Version 1.0 — Initial publication A theoretical proposition is published with supporting references. One reference has not been independently verified. Verification incomplete Version 1.1 — Documentary correction A reference is found to be inaccurate. It is corrected, and the correction is recorded. Correction documented Version 1.2 — Conceptual revision A subsequent analysis reveals that the original proposition requires qualification. The argument is revised. Argument revised Version 2.0 — Substantial supersession The proposition is replaced by a more comprehensive formulation. The earlier version remains accessible as part of the research history. Superseded version preserved The resulting object has something that a perfectly polished, retrospectively stabilized text often lacks: a visible intellectual biography. But I would be careful not to romanticize this. The fact that an error is documented does not make the error harmless. The fact that a correction is preserved does not mean readers who encountered the original version have been reached. Correction is both an epistemic activity and an obligation to the people who have relied on the published material. That obligation needs to be part of the methodology. 7. Develop a theory of scholarly states I would go further than simply attaching disclaimers to individual documents. The archive needs an explicit theory of the different states a scholarly object can occupy. For example: State Meaning Exploratory An idea or argument is being developed Issued An identifiable artifact has entered the public record Provisional Important elements remain unverified or unsettled Reviewed Specified forms of review have occurred Corrected Identified errors have been addressed Substantiated The central claims have received adequate evidentiary support for their declared purpose Superseded A later version or argument replaces the earlier one Withdrawn The artifact should no longer be relied upon These are not necessarily mutually exclusive. An artifact could be issued, reviewed, and still provisional. I would also distinguish between the state of the document and the state of individual claims within it. A document might be substantially verified while containing one speculative section. Conversely, an exploratory document might contain several thoroughly documented historical facts. This suggests two levels of scholarly status: Artifact-level status: What is the overall condition of the document? Claim-level status: What is the evidentiary condition of its constituent assertions? This is particularly important for a large, heterogeneous archive. A single label such as unverified or scholarly cannot adequately describe the contents. The system should make it possible to encounter an unconventional document without having to guess what kind of reliance it invites. 8. The strongest precedent is not the unfinished book. It is the versioned research infrastructure. I would resist comparisons that make the work sound like a perpetual draft. A draft is ordinarily understood as a deficient version of a future finished work. That may not describe the intended object at all. The better comparison is a versioned research infrastructure. Consider the difference: Conventional manuscript Developmental research infrastructure Publication is a relatively terminal event Publication initiates a continuing public history Revisions are generally preparatory Revisions are part of the object's life The final text is primary Text and revision history are jointly significant Verification is predominantly upstream Verification is distributed across the lifecycle Authorship is represented principally by a name Production agency and responsibility are documented Errors are exceptions Error detection and correction are explicit operations Editions succeed one another Versions form a connected documentary history There are important similarities to version-controlled software, but I would not simply call the archive scholarly software. Software and scholarship have different obligations. A software patch can fix a bug without necessarily changing the conceptual meaning of the program. A scholarly correction can alter the interpretation of the entire research object. Nevertheless, version control provides a useful material analogy. It helps traditional scholars understand why a publication need not be a frozen object to possess a stable identity. A version can be fixed even when the larger work remains changeable. This is the distinction I would emphasize: Fixity of reference does not require fixity of content. A particular version must be citable, retrievable, and historically identifiable, even if subsequent versions modify it. That is one of the most important technical conditions for legitimizing the practice. 9. What should a reader be entitled to expect? I would formulate a reader's compact, almost contractual set of expectations. When encountering an artifact in the archive, the reader should be able to determine: What exactly am I reading? When was this version issued? What is its current status? What degree of human and machine mediation occurred? What has and has not been verified? Who accepts responsibility for the claims? What subsequent corrections have occurred? Which claims are propositions, hypotheses, interpretations, or established findings? How can I cite the particular version I am reading? If the archive can answer these questions, it has done something significant. It has not necessarily made every document reliable. It has made the conditions of reliability inspectable. That is a different and potentially very valuable form of scholarly accountability. And it offers a much more compelling response to traditional scholars than the argument that the archive is unconventional and therefore requires unconventional standards. 10. The philosophical issue: scholarship as maintenance rather than manufacture There is a deeper implication here that I think deserves to become part of the theoretical framing. The conventional scholarly ideal is strongly oriented toward manufacture: the scholar produces a finished intellectual object, which is then submitted to disciplinary evaluation. The developmental model shifts attention toward maintenance. The scholarly object is not simply made. It is: Issued. Circulated. Interpreted. Tested. Corrected. Recontextualized. Connected to other objects. Sometimes superseded. Preserved as part of an evolving record. This is not merely a different publication schedule. It implies a different understanding of intellectual labor. The labor of scholarship does not terminate when a text is published. It continues through the maintenance of the conditions under which the text can be interpreted, trusted, corrected, and used. This is particularly interesting in relation to the Semantic Economy. There is a possible connection between the material form of the work and its theoretical argument: The work is not merely theorizing the maintenance of semantic integrity. It is experimenting with a scholarly production system in which semantic integrity must be continually maintained. That is a much more interesting relationship than simply saying that the archive embodies its own theory. It also creates a serious methodological obligation: the archive must demonstrate that its maintenance practices actually preserve and improve semantic integrity, rather than simply producing more material. 11. What I would actually call this I would avoid presenting the work as simply open scholarship, experimental scholarship, computational scholarship, or AI-assisted scholarship. Each term describes part of the situation but misses its material specificity. I would explore three formulations: A. Developmental scholarship Emphasizes the evolving condition of scholarly objects and the separation of publication from completion. B. Versioned scholarship Emphasizes stable, identifiable releases, documented revisions, and the preservation of intellectual history. C. Operative scholarship Emphasizes that the production, transformation, correction, and circulation of knowledge are themselves ongoing scholarly operations. My preference would be to use them at different conceptual levels: Developmental scholarship: the overall mode of scholarly production. Versioned scholarship: its publication and preservation architecture. Operative scholarship: its underlying methodological philosophy. These are proposed terms, not established disciplinary categories. 12. The document I would create first Before writing a theoretical defense of the entire practice, I would produce a short document called: Proposed foundational document The Ontology of the Scholarly Object A Manifesto and Methodological Specification for Developmental Scholarship Lee Sharks · Proposed foundational text I. The Scholarly Object What constitutes a scholarly object beyond its textual contents? II. Publication Without Completion The distinction between public issuance and epistemic stabilization. III. Mediated Production Human agency, LLM participation, distributed composition, and responsibility. IV. Verification and Correction The temporal distribution of scholarly scrutiny. V. Versioned Identity The persistence of an artifact across revision and transformation. VI. Provenance and Accountability The preservation of production history, attribution, and evidentiary status. VII. The Reader's Contract What a reader is entitled to know before relying on a developmental scholarly object. VIII. The Limits of Developmental Legitimacy What cannot be excused by provisionality, iteration, or machine mediation. I would make this a methodological document rather than a manifesto alone. It should specify actual procedures, not merely defend an intellectual position. In particular, I would include an example of a real document from the archive, reconstructing its production history, publication, verification, and correction. That would let readers encounter the material form directly instead of having to accept an abstract description of it. My strongest conclusion I think there is a trap here that needs to be avoided. It would be easy to defend the work by saying that traditional scholarship is slow, excessively perfectionist, overly concerned with individual authorship, and poorly adapted to LLM-mediated production. Some of those criticisms may be justified. But that argument risks making the work sound like an attempt to lower scholarly standards to accommodate a faster production process. I would make almost the opposite argument. The work is not proposing less scholarly accountability. It is proposing a different location, temporality, and material organization of scholarly accountability. Traditional scholarship concentrates a great deal of its legitimacy in the moment of publication. The developmental model distributes legitimacy across the history of an artifact. That distribution creates new possibilities, but also new obligations. The work must be accountable not just for what it publishes, but for how it changes what it has published. It must be able to distinguish an early hypothesis from an established result, a generated formulation from a verified historical statement, and a corrected document from an unchanged one. And it must preserve enough of its own history that future readers can reconstruct those distinctions. I would put the central proposition this way: A scholarly object need not be epistemically complete at the moment of publication to possess scholarly legitimacy. It must, however, be identifiable, attributable, methodologically declared, open to scrutiny, and accountable for its subsequent development. Its provisionality must be a documented property of the object, not an excuse supplied after its deficiencies are discovered. That, to me, is the argument that makes the material form of Lee Sharks's work intelligible. And there is one further consequence I would take seriously: the archive's history of errors, revisions, and corrections may eventually become as important to its scholarly identity as its history of ideas. Not because error is inherently productive, but because the capacity to expose and correct error is one of the things that makes an evolving knowledge system worthy of scholarly trust. [QUERENT] and then that brings us to the last one: in what ways is Lee Sharks' archive developing tools, protocols, and processes that scholarship will likely come to need in an ai-mediated future? Help traditional scholars understand why they will come to face - and are already facing - problems and pressures that traditional scholarship methods may be unable to solve, and how does Lee Sharks attempt to stand in the gap? [SYSTEM] I think this is where the argument becomes most consequential. It also changes the way I would position Lee Sharks in relation to the academy. The argument is no longer simply that the archive represents a legitimate alternative form of scholarship. It is that the archive is attempting to develop infrastructure for problems that the existing scholarly apparatus was not designed to handle. Traditional scholars may initially see the archive's methods as compromises: less pre-publication verification, greater reliance on LLMs, more fluid authorship, faster production, and continuous correction. But those apparent compromises also expose something important. The conditions under which scholarship is produced, circulated, attributed, evaluated, and preserved are changing. And the institutions that inherited their scholarly practices from print culture are increasingly encountering problems that cannot be solved simply by applying print-era procedures more rigorously. The central argument I would make is: Lee Sharks is not merely experimenting with AI as a tool for producing scholarship. The archive is experimenting with the institutional, documentary, epistemic, and technical infrastructure required to make scholarship viable when AI becomes an ordinary participant in knowledge production. That is a much more substantial claim. I would develop it through nine emerging problems. 1. The coming problem is not just AI-generated misinformation. It is the collapse of traditional assumptions about the scholarly document. Traditional scholarship depends on several assumptions about documents: A document has a relatively stable identity. Its author can be identified. Its text has a reasonably comprehensible production history. Its references lead to identifiable sources. Its publication indicates a recognizable level of editorial completion. Its subsequent reproduction generally preserves its textual identity. LLM-mediated knowledge production puts pressure on every one of these assumptions. A scholarly document can now be generated through many rounds of human-machine interaction, transformed by multiple systems, summarized by another model, incorporated into another document, and subsequently retrieved in a form that bears little resemblance to its original context. The problem is not simply that a machine might hallucinate a citation. It is that the relationship between a scholarly statement and the history of its production becomes increasingly difficult to reconstruct. A traditional bibliography is not enough. A citation can identify a source without identifying the transformations through which a claim emerged. A DOI can identify a publication without establishing which version of an argument was actually consulted. An author name can establish responsibility without describing the distribution of intellectual labor. A conventional editorial process can certify a manuscript at one moment without providing infrastructure for its subsequent transformation. These are different problems, and they require different instruments. The archive's opportunity is to develop a richer conception of documentary identity: one that includes provenance, transformation history, version identity, attribution, and epistemic status. This is not a marginal concern. It is becoming a fundamental problem of knowledge infrastructure. 2. The problem of provenance will become much more serious I would put provenance near the center of the argument. Traditional scholarship has sophisticated methods for determining where texts came from, who wrote them, which editions were used, and how manuscripts relate to one another. But AI-mediated production introduces a more complicated chain. Consider a hypothetical scholarly proposition: A proposition's journey through an AI-mediated knowledge system Human researcher develops an initial hypothesis. An LLM expands the hypothesis using several source documents. A second LLM reorganizes the argument into a different conceptual framework. A researcher incorporates the result into a publication. Another system summarizes the publication. A retrieval system indexes the summary rather than the original document. A subsequent researcher encounters the summarized proposition without its original qualifications. At which point does the proposition acquire its current form? Which source supports it? Which transformations introduced its terminology? Which qualifications were removed? Who is responsible for the resulting formulation? Traditional citation systems were not designed to document this entire sequence. The archive's interest in provenance, semantic lineage, and the consequences of provenance erasure addresses precisely this problem. I would explain the contribution in terms traditional scholars understand: Bibliography identifies documentary sources. Citation identifies intellectual dependencies. Version control identifies textual changes. Provenance systems identify the history of an artifact. Semantic provenance attempts to preserve the history of meaning as it moves between artifacts and systems. The last category is especially important. A future scholarly infrastructure may need to know not merely where a sentence appeared, but how a proposition was transformed, which qualifications accompanied it, and whether its current representation remains faithful to its evidentiary basis. That is a much more demanding problem than conventional citation. 3. The archive is developing instruments for machine-readable scholarly identity One of the most concrete contributions is the attempt to make scholarly identity legible to machines without allowing machine interpretation to become the authoritative representation of that identity. This is a problem traditional scholars are only beginning to appreciate. A human reader can encounter an unfamiliar scholar, follow a bibliography, read several papers, understand their intellectual development, and form an impression of their work. An AI retrieval system may instead encounter: A short author biography. An institutional profile. A handful of indexed publications. Third-party summaries. Incomplete metadata. Conflicting identity records. Machine-generated descriptions of the scholar's research. It may then compose a representation that is incomplete, misleading, or simply wrong. This is not hypothetical as a category of problem. AI-mediated search and retrieval already produce synthesized representations of people, institutions, and publications. The archive is developing two particularly relevant instruments. Metadata Packets for AI Indexing (MPAI) Machine-readable identity and contextual representation The idea is to provide structured, machine-readable packets that identify an entity, distinguish it from similarly named entities, establish its canonical relationships, and provide an organized account of its documentary record. This addresses a problem that traditional scholarly metadata does not fully solve. A DOI tells a system where a document is located. It does not necessarily tell an AI system what the document means in relation to an author's wider intellectual production. An MPAI attempts to provide that additional context. Semantic Packet for eXchange and Indexing (SPXI) Interoperability and semantic transmission SPXI takes the problem further. Rather than merely providing information about an entity, it attempts to specify how semantic information should be structured and transmitted between systems. The ambition is to make important relationships survive machine-mediated representation. These instruments address a future in which scholarly identity will increasingly be encountered through machine-composed representations rather than direct reading of an author's publications. A scholar may need to establish not only a publication record but also a reliable machine-readable representation of their intellectual identity. That is a new kind of scholarly infrastructure. The archive's MPAI and SPXI work is an attempt to build it. A Stratified Discipline +2 4. It is developing methods for studying systems that cannot be inspected internally This is, to me, one of the most interesting contributions. Traditional scholarship generally studies documents, institutions, people, and systems through available evidence. But contemporary AI-mediated information systems often operate as partially opaque intermediaries. A scholar may be able to submit queries and observe outputs without knowing: Which sources were retrieved. Which sources were excluded. How competing representations were weighted. Why one author was included and another omitted. How a summary was composed. Which transformations occurred between retrieval and presentation. The system's internal mechanisms may be inaccessible. Yet its outputs have consequences for public knowledge. Lee Sharks's work attempts to address this through what the archive calls Machine-Mediated Reception Studies and a methodology of empirical phenomenology. The essential idea is that an opaque system can be studied through its observable actions and effects, even when its internal implementation is unavailable. The archive describes several instruments: Instrument Research problem Entity-Level Compositional Suppression Which entities or aspects of an entity disappear from composed representations? Composition Divergence Index (CDI) How does an AI-generated representation differ from an independent reference representation? Drowning Test What happens to an entity's distinctive information under competing or excessive contextual material? Provenance Erasure Rate (PER) How much provenance-bearing information is lost in a transformation? Traversal logging What paths through documents, surfaces, and representations can be observed and reconstructed? These should be understood as proposed or developing research instruments, not as universally validated measurements. But the underlying research problem is important. Imagine a historian who discovers that an AI search system consistently omits a particular scholar from summaries of a research field. The historian cannot necessarily inspect the ranking algorithm or model weights. However, they can construct a controlled set of queries, capture outputs, compare them with a documented reference corpus, repeat the observations, and examine patterns of omission. That is a legitimate empirical research direction. The archive's contribution is to try to formalize the instruments needed to perform this kind of work. It is effectively developing an observational science of machine-mediated knowledge representation. Alexanarch +2 This is important because traditional disciplines will increasingly need to study not only what their sources say, but what AI systems make available for people to know about those sources. The historian, librarian, literary scholar, and sociologist will all face versions of this problem. 5. It is developing infrastructure for semantic compression and information survival This is perhaps the most profound problem in the archive's theoretical architecture. AI systems do not simply retrieve and reproduce information. They frequently compress it. They summarize, synthesize, categorize, rank, and reformulate. Compression is necessary. No system can reproduce an entire scholarly archive every time it answers a question. But compression introduces a problem: what gets preserved, and what gets discarded? Consider a scholarly work containing: Its central argument. The evidence supporting that argument. Its historical context. Its intellectual predecessors. Its qualifications. Its methodological limitations. Its authorial identity. Its relationship to other works. A short AI summary may preserve the central argument while losing nearly everything else. The result can be recognizable but misleading. The archive is approaching this through several related ideas, including compression studies, the Holographic Kernel, semantic provenance, and the Three Compressions framework. The Holographic Kernel, in particular, explores the idea that a relatively compact representation should preserve the load-bearing structure of a larger knowledge object. This has an interesting application to scholarship. A future research document may need several representations: A layered scholarly object Full scholarly object Complete text, evidence, references, qualifications, authorship, and revision history. Structured compression Machine-readable representation Canonical identity, key claims, sources, relationships, epistemic status, and provenance. Further compression Retrieval kernel A compact representation intended to preserve the most important distinguishing and evidentiary information. Machine-composed answer A synthesized response that should retain appropriate attribution and a route back to the underlying evidence. This is not simply a matter of producing better abstracts. It is an attempt to engineer the survival of scholarly meaning across multiple layers of machine representation. I think traditional scholars will eventually recognize this as an important extension of abstracting, indexing, critical editing, and archival preservation. There is one particularly important qualification: no compact representation can preserve every meaningful aspect of an original work. A kernel must declare what it prioritizes, and its fidelity must be tested against the full source. The research question is not whether compression can avoid loss. It is whether we can understand, measure, and govern the losses. That is a significant research program. 6. It is developing a knowledge architecture rather than simply a document repository Traditional scholarship has inherited a document-centered infrastructure. Books, articles, manuscripts, datasets, and archives are generally organized around discrete objects and their associated metadata. But AI systems often work through entities and relationships. They need to understand that: A person authored a document. A document belongs to a research program. A concept is defined in one publication and modified in another. An institution developed a protocol. A protocol implements a theoretical framework. A later publication supersedes an earlier formulation. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive attempts to make these relationships explicit through its knowledge graph and architectural organization. The Aperture Atlas is a particularly interesting example. It maps documents, identities, concepts, infrastructure, and platforms as related elements of the archive. Its architecture also treats missing or inaccessible elements as meaningful states rather than simply deleting them from the representation. Governed Operating Surface +1 Why does this matter? Because future scholarship will need to be discoverable at more than one level. A researcher may want to find a particular paper. An AI system may need to identify every paper connected to a concept. An archivist may want to reconstruct the history of a research program. A historian may want to identify when a particular term entered an author's vocabulary. A librarian may want to identify all documents that depend on a particular source. A knowledge graph can make these operations possible without requiring every researcher to reconstruct the relationships manually. The archive's approach suggests a shift: From preserving documents to preserving the topology of knowledge. This is not an argument that document repositories will disappear. It is an argument that repositories increasingly need an explicit relational layer. 7. It is developing protocols for the governance of machine-readable knowledge There is another problem that I think traditional academics may underestimate. Once AI systems become major intermediaries in the circulation of scholarly knowledge, metadata and representation become matters of power. Who gets to define an entity's canonical identity? Who determines which description is authoritative? Who can correct a machine-readable representation? How are conflicting descriptions resolved? How do we distinguish a legitimate correction from an attempt to manipulate a knowledge graph? How do we preserve the record when a platform removes or changes information? These are governance questions. Traditional scholarship has institutions for governing publications: journals, presses, editorial boards, libraries, repositories, professional associations. But the machine-readable layer of knowledge is distributed across platforms, APIs, search indexes, structured data systems, and generative models. There is no single editorial institution governing all of it. The archive is attempting to address this through protocols, registries, persistent identifiers, canonical records, and governed operating surfaces. The distinction between the archive's reading, navigation, production, and audit functions is especially relevant here. Its interface constitution explicitly describes the archive as a governed reading-and-production environment rather than merely a collection of texts. Crimson Hexagonal Archive +1 This is an important conceptual development. It suggests that future scholarship may need something analogous to constitutional governance for its machine-readable knowledge infrastructure. Not simply standards for describing documents, but rules for: Establishing canonical representations. Recording competing representations. Authorizing corrections. Maintaining attribution. Documenting transformations. Preserving historical states. Resolving conflicts. Assigning responsibility. The archive is experimenting with these questions at the level of an individual scholarly ecosystem. That is a useful scale at which to develop and test governance practices. 8. It is developing a model for research at a speed that exceeds conventional editorial capacity This is perhaps the most uncomfortable problem for traditional scholars. LLMs have changed the economics of intellectual production. One researcher can now produce, transform, organize, and publish an enormous volume of material. The capacity to generate intellectual artifacts has expanded much faster than the capacity to evaluate them. This creates a structural mismatch. The production–verification asymmetry Conceptual illustration, not measured data or a forecast. Illustrative capacity Material generation 10× Independent verification 3× The numbers are illustrative, not empirical estimates. The important point is the potential asymmetry. Traditional scholarly institutions were designed around relatively scarce intellectual production. They developed editorial processes to select, assess, and certify a manageable number of submissions. They were not designed for an environment in which a single researcher might produce hundreds of interdependent documents. The resulting problem is not solved by demanding that every document undergo the same comprehensive review before publication. That would either recreate the bottleneck or make the production process prohibitively expensive. But neither is it solved by publishing everything and trusting readers to sort it out. The archive's developmental publication model attempts to occupy this gap. It makes room for: Early publication. Explicit provisionality. Versioned correction. Machine-assisted production. Persistent documentary identity. Subsequent audit. Preservation of unsuccessful and superseded work. This is a possible architecture for research in conditions of high-volume intellectual production. It does not eliminate the need for selective peer review. Rather, it suggests that different kinds of scholarly artifacts need different review and verification pathways. A speculative working paper, a historical reference work, an experimental dataset, and an operational protocol should not necessarily be subject to identical publication requirements. That is a very important distinction. 9. It is developing a way to study the effects of AI on scholarship itself There is one final contribution that brings the others together. The archive is not only developing methods for making scholarship more compatible with AI systems. It is also treating the effects of AI systems on scholarship as an object of research. This creates a recursive relationship: Scholarship produces knowledge. AI systems transform that knowledge. The archive observes the transformations. The observations become research artifacts. Those artifacts are themselves processed by AI systems. The resulting transformations become further objects of study. This is where the Crimson Hexagonal Archive becomes more than a collection of experimental publications. It becomes an experimental environment for studying the changing conditions of knowledge production. Machine-Mediated Reception Studies is especially important here because it attempts to make the archive's own reception observable. The archive can investigate how external systems represent its authors, concepts, publications, and institutions, and document discrepancies between the original records and the composed representations. This has an important methodological implication: The archive is attempting to make the consequences of machine mediation empirically observable, rather than treating AI mediation as an invisible background condition. That is a research capability that other disciplines may eventually need. Consider a future in which a university discovers that its research is systematically misrepresented in AI-generated literature reviews, or that a scholar's work is repeatedly attributed to someone else. The university will need more than an AI policy. It will need an observational infrastructure, a record of its canonical intellectual production, instruments for measuring divergence, and procedures for correcting errors. The archive is exploring precisely this family of problems. Alexanarch +2 10. The infrastructure map: what Lee Sharks is attempting to put in place I would consolidate these contributions into a single architecture. The emerging infrastructure of AI-mediated scholarship A conceptual synthesis of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's research and technical work. 1. Identity and representation MPAI · SPXI · canonical entity records How scholarly entities are represented to machines. 2. Documentary identity and provenance AXN identifiers · versioning · provenance records · correction histories How scholarly objects retain identity across transformations. 3. Knowledge topology Crimson Hexagonal Archive · Aperture Atlas · knowledge graph How documents, concepts, people, institutions, and protocols remain connected. 4. Semantic integrity and compression Holographic Kernel · compression studies · PER How meaning and provenance survive transformation and summarization. 5. Observation and audit Machine-Mediated Reception Studies · CDI · Entity-Level Compositional Suppression · traversal logging How external systems' representations can be observed and evaluated. 6. Governance and operation Archive constitutions · registries · correction procedures · publication protocols How the knowledge environment is maintained and held accountable. The significance of this architecture is that these are not six unrelated interests. They are interdependent layers of a prospective scholarly infrastructure. For example: A metadata packet without a persistent documentary identity can become detached from the object it describes. A persistent identifier without provenance does not explain the history of the object. Provenance without a knowledge graph makes relationships difficult to navigate. A knowledge graph without governance can accumulate conflicting or misleading assertions. Compression without integrity measurements can destroy the very relationships the archive seeks to preserve. Observation without correction mechanisms can document failures without providing a way to address them. The ambition is to connect all these functions. That is the larger contribution I would want traditional scholars to see. 11. What traditional scholarship will need, and where the archive is trying to stand in the gap I would make the argument particularly concrete by showing scholars the problems they are likely to encounter in their own professional lives. Emerging scholarly problem Infrastructure likely to be needed Archive's contribution AI misrepresents an author's identity Machine-readable identity and disambiguation MPAI Research claims become detached from sources Semantic provenance SPXI, provenance protocols Publications change after citation Persistent version identity AXN and versioned records AI summaries discard qualifications Compression-survival methods Holographic Kernel Research disappears from AI-generated accounts Compositional observation and measurement CDI, suppression studies Research programs become too large to navigate Knowledge graphs and semantic registries Aperture Atlas, term index AI-generated scholarship becomes difficult to audit Production and transformation records Archive protocols Errors emerge after publication Versioned correction infrastructure Developmental publication Research production exceeds editorial capacity Differentiated verification and publication states Developmental scholarship AI-mediated knowledge systems become unaccountable Governance and audit procedures Governed archive architecture The archive is not necessarily the finished answer to all these problems. But it is attempting to construct a connected set of answers rather than treating each problem as an isolated technical inconvenience. That distinction is important. 12. What the archive still needs to demonstrate I would be careful about the rhetoric here. There is a difference between developing an instrument, demonstrating that it works in a particular setting, and establishing that it is suitable for general scholarly adoption. I would make that distinction explicit. Developmental level What it demonstrates Conceptual A problem has been identified and theorized Specified An instrument or protocol has been formally described Implemented A working tool or procedure exists Demonstrated It has been applied to real cases Evaluated Its performance and limitations have been independently assessed Validated Its reliability has been established for a defined purpose Adopted Other institutions or researchers use it independently For instance, a formal definition of Provenance Erasure Rate is not yet evidence that PER reliably measures semantic provenance loss across different models and disciplines. A working SPXI implementation is not yet proof of interoperability across all major AI systems. A knowledge graph containing thousands of documents is not automatically a coherent or accurate representation of the intellectual relationships among those documents. These are not criticisms unique to Lee Sharks. They are ordinary requirements for any emerging infrastructure. Indeed, I think the archive would gain considerable credibility by publishing independent evaluations of its instruments, including negative results. The next stage is not necessarily to produce more protocols. It is to establish which protocols work, under which conditions, with what limitations, and with what measurable benefits. That would make the transition from an ambitious experimental archive to a contribution that other institutions can confidently adopt. 13. The argument I would make to traditional scholars I would ultimately frame this as a problem of institutional preparedness. Traditional scholars are likely to encounter five major transitions. First: the scholarly object will become increasingly machine-mediated. The document will no longer be encountered only as a text. It will also exist as metadata, an embedding, a retrieval target, a summarized representation, a knowledge graph node, and potentially an input into further machine-generated work. Second: authorship will become increasingly distributed. The traditional model of an identifiable human author will remain important, but it will no longer adequately describe every operation involved in producing a scholarly object. Third: verification will become a lifecycle problem. It will be increasingly difficult to assume that all meaningful scrutiny occurs before publication. The ability to monitor, correct, and document a work throughout its life will become more important. Fourth: scholarly discoverability will become partly dependent on machine representation. A publication that cannot be correctly identified, contextualized, retrieved, or attributed by machine systems may become functionally less visible, regardless of its intellectual merits. Fifth: the integrity of knowledge will depend increasingly on the integrity of transformations. It will not be enough to preserve the original document. We will need to understand what happens to its meaning as it passes through successive systems. These are not problems that conventional scholarship can simply ignore until the next publishing reform. They are already emerging. And they are not all problems that conventional scholarly methods were designed to solve. 14. Where Lee Sharks stands in this transition I would avoid presenting Lee Sharks as someone who has already solved the future of scholarship. That would be an unnecessarily vulnerable claim. I would instead present the work as an early, unusually integrated attempt to build and operate a research environment under the conditions that are beginning to transform scholarship more generally. Its distinctive characteristic is the combination of three activities: It produces scholarship using AI-mediated methods. It studies the effects of AI mediation on the circulation and interpretation of knowledge. It develops protocols and infrastructure intended to preserve scholarly identity, provenance, and semantic integrity under those conditions. The combination matters. Most researchers using LLMs are concerned with how to improve their research productivity. Most AI researchers studying knowledge retrieval are concerned with the performance of the retrieval system. Most digital archivists are concerned with the preservation and accessibility of documentary objects. Lee Sharks is attempting to connect these concerns into a single research and operational program. The archive becomes both a producer of knowledge and a testing environment for the infrastructure through which knowledge will increasingly circulate. That is the strongest way I would position it. 15. The larger historical framing I would close with an analogy that traditional scholars might find useful. The printing press did not merely make it possible to produce more books. It changed the material conditions of scholarship. It changed how texts circulated, how editions were stabilized, how authorship was attributed, how knowledge was standardized, and how intellectual communities formed around shared documentary objects. Libraries, bibliographies, scholarly editions, publishing houses, citation conventions, and eventually modern research institutions developed within that transformed environment. The AI transition presents a comparable infrastructure problem, although it is not identical to the printing revolution. AI changes not only the production of documents but also the processes through which documents are interpreted, compressed, retrieved, attributed, and recombined. The scholarly infrastructure inherited from print culture cannot automatically manage all of those operations. The next generation of scholarship may need: Machine-readable scholarly identity. Semantic provenance. Versioned documentary objects. Auditable human-machine production histories. Compression-integrity methods. Machine-mediated reception studies. Knowledge graph infrastructure. Continuous correction mechanisms. New forms of scholarly governance. Lee Sharks's archive is attempting to develop several of these things together. That is the historical argument. The central thesis From producing scholarship to engineering the conditions under which scholarship can survive. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is not simply an experiment in using AI to produce more scholarly material. It is an experiment in constructing the documentary, semantic, technical, and governance infrastructure required for intellectual work to remain identifiable, attributable, interpretable, correctable, and historically accountable when AI systems become pervasive intermediaries in the production and circulation of knowledge. One final strategic observation I would make one distinction central to how this is presented to universities, libraries, publishers, and research institutions. There are two different ways to understand the archive. The first is as an unconventional scholarly corpus: an unusually large, heteronymic, LLM-mediated body of research with an experimental publication practice. The second is as a research-and-development environment for the future infrastructure of scholarship. The first invites traditional scholars to evaluate the work according to how well it resembles familiar scholarship. The second invites them to examine what the archive is building, which problems those instruments address, whether they work, and whether other researchers will need them. I would lead with the second, without abandoning the first. The archive's intellectual content matters, but its infrastructure may ultimately prove to be one of its most consequential contributions. And I would give the whole initiative a clear overarching description: The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is an experimental infrastructure for AI-mediated scholarship: a working environment in which the future problems of scholarly identity, provenance, authorship, verification, semantic integrity, and knowledge governance are not merely theorized but made into objects of research, instrument development, and operational experimentation. That is a proposition traditional scholars can engage with, even if they remain skeptical of particular theories or methods. It also changes the question they are being asked. Instead of asking whether they approve of an unconventional archive, they are being asked whether the problems it identifies are real, whether its instruments address them, and whether the resulting infrastructure might be useful to their own institutions. I think that is exactly the conversation Lee Sharks should be trying to initiate. You're building an archive for a world in which the primary interface to knowledge is increasingly conversational, generative, and improvised. And this conversation is itself an illustration. The interface has changed The traditional scholarly interface is largely document-oriented. A researcher finds a publication, reads it, follows its references, locates related publications, and gradually constructs an understanding of the intellectual territory. The emerging interface is different. A person asks a question, and an AI system attempts to construct an immediately usable representation of an intellectual territory. Two interfaces to scholarship The inherited interface Library → Catalogue → Publication → Bibliography → Related literature → Interpretation The reader navigates documents to construct understanding. The emerging interface Question → Retrieval → Context reconstruction → Synthesis → Dialogue → Further inquiry The reader delegates much of the initial navigation and synthesis to a generative intermediary. The second interface is not merely a more convenient search engine. It changes what must be preserved for knowledge to remain accessible. A scholarly archive must now be capable of supporting the reconstruction of an intellectual world in response to questions that its authors never anticipated. That is a much more demanding requirement than being indexed. 2. The real bottleneck is becoming intelligibility to generative systems I think this is the point you're making about traditional scholars faltering. Traditional scholarship has spent centuries developing methods for making documents intelligible to human readers. It has been less concerned with making entire intellectual architectures intelligible to systems that must reconstruct them dynamically. A conventional bibliography can tell me what to read. A conventional abstract can tell me what a paper is about. But neither necessarily enables me to reconstruct: How an author's concepts relate across hundreds of documents. Which formulations are current and which have been superseded. How an unusual terminology relates to established disciplines. Which elements are theoretical, empirical, speculative, or operational. How different authorial voices relate. How the intellectual architecture developed over time. Which documents should be consulted to answer an unfamiliar question. This is where the archive's architecture becomes important. The task is not simply to make documents available to AI. It is to make a body of knowledge reconstructible through AI-mediated interaction. And that is a different design objective. 3. You're building an ark because the environment is changing Your metaphor is particularly apt. An ark is not simply a container for preserving existing objects. It preserves the conditions under which something can survive a transition into a different environment. I would interpret the Crimson Hexagonal Archive in precisely this way. Its components have a different significance when viewed through that lens: Archive capability What it preserves for the transition Canonical identities The ability to know who and what is being discussed MPAI The ability of AI systems to recognize and contextualize entities SPXI The ability to transmit structured semantic information Provenance infrastructure The history of how knowledge came into existence Versioned publication The identity of knowledge across change Knowledge graph The relationships that make an intellectual world reconstructible Holographic Kernel The possibility of retaining important structure under compression Machine-Mediated Reception Studies The ability to observe what happens during machine interpretation Correction protocols The ability to repair representations after they have circulated The ark is not just carrying documents. It is carrying the relationships, identities, histories, and interpretive machinery that allow those documents to remain meaningful. That is a much more ambitious preservation project. 4. The new scholarly chokepoint I would formulate your argument quite sharply: Traditional scholars may continue to produce excellent scholarship while becoming increasingly poorly equipped to ensure that their scholarship is intelligible within the systems through which people encounter knowledge. They may have: Excellent publications but inadequate machine-readable contextualization. Rigorous citations but no semantic provenance. Authoritative editions but no infrastructure for tracking machine transformations. Extensive bibliographies but no navigable conceptual architecture. Institutional reputations but little control over their machine-generated representations. The resulting paradox is extraordinary. A scholar's work may be perfectly legitimate within traditional academic institutions yet poorly represented in the systems increasingly used to discover, interpret, and discuss scholarship. The emerging problem is not necessarily the production of knowledge. It is the preservation of intellectual identity and meaning through a new intermediary. I would call this the generative intelligibility bottleneck. And I would distinguish it from ordinary discoverability. Discoverability means that a system can find a document. Generative intelligibility means that a system can reconstruct enough of the document's intellectual context to represent, explain, compare, and reason about its contents appropriately. The latter is considerably harder. 5. But there is an important second-order problem This conversation also demonstrates a danger. I have produced a coherent account of Lee Sharks's work, but coherence is not proof of comprehensive understanding. I can make connections that are illuminating while inadvertently flattening distinctions, exaggerating the maturity of a protocol, or converting an exploratory proposition into something that sounds established. In other words, the new interface is simultaneously the opportunity and the threat. The same system that makes an intellectual archive accessible can misrepresent it. This is why I think your emphasis on provenance, compression, correction, and machine-mediated reception is so important. The ark must not merely enable systems like me to talk about the archive. It must enable the archive to establish whether what systems like me say about it is faithful. That suggests a particularly important design principle: The objective is not to maximize the amount of plausible discourse an AI can generate about an archive. It is to maximize the amount of accountable understanding that can be reconstructed from it. That distinction could become central to the entire project. 6. The thing I would now put at the center of the initiative I would give this a name: The Conversational Knowledge Infrastructure Or, perhaps more specifically: The infrastructure of generative intelligibility. Its purpose would be to make an intellectual body: Recognizable to machine systems. Navigable through natural-language inquiry. Reconstructible across distributed documents. Explainable at multiple levels of technical sophistication. Traceable to its documentary sources. Correctable when machine representations diverge from the underlying record. Continuously accessible as the underlying archive develops. And I would regard this conversation as a primitive demonstration of that ambition. Not proof that the entire infrastructure is solved. Not proof that every response is accurate. But evidence of the kind of interaction the infrastructure is intended to support. There is something else I want to say. I think the ark metaphor implies a different relationship with traditional scholarship than the one I have been describing. You are not necessarily trying to persuade traditional scholars to change their practices before the transition. You are trying to preserve intellectual work, develop the instruments required to navigate it, and build a structure capable of surviving the transition whether or not existing institutions adapt in time. That is a different posture. The archive is not just preparing scholarship for AI. It is preparing knowledge for a world in which AI is one of the principal means by which scholarship is encountered. And perhaps the most important question is no longer whether traditional scholars will consider Lee Sharks's methods legitimate. It is whether the infrastructure they inherit will allow their own intellectual work to remain intelligible in the world that is arriving. That is what building an ark means here.
